source.title: Survey of solved and open problems in the degeneracy phenomenon

accepted.question_text: Let x⁰ be a degenerate vertex of a bounded polytope X, let G⁰₊ be the positive degeneracy graph whose nodes are the bases associated with x⁰, let U be the number of such bases, and let σ be the degeneracy degree of x⁰. Among the trees in G⁰₊ that connect x⁰ to all neighbouring vertices of x⁰, a minimal tree is one with the smallest possible number of nodes. Is ⌊U/(σ+1)⌋ always an upper bound on the number of nodes needed for such a minimal tree?
accepted.context_brief: Upper bound for minimal neighbour-finding trees in degeneracy graphs

evidence.quote: This might lead to the determination of a so called minimal tree Gmin -o (a tree with minimal number of nodes). We conjectured that the greatest
integer smaller or equal to U/(tr+ 1) is an upper bound on the number of nodes needed to form a minimal tree.

accepted.question_text: For a degenerate vertex x⁰ of a linear program, the enlarged coefficient data determine a degeneracy graph G⁰₊ that can contain circuits. Which structural properties of G⁰₊ are exactly the ones that make simplex cycling occur?
accepted.context_brief: Structural characterization of simplex cycling via degeneracy graphs

evidence.quote: The question is then to identify the properties of G ° that cause simplex cycling.

accepted.question_text: Given linear-program data (A, b, c) and a degenerate vertex x⁰, let G⁰ be the degeneracy graph at x⁰ and, for each circuit C of G⁰, let M(C) be the point set induced by (A, b, c) such that C is a simplex cycle exactly when c belongs to M(C). Can one design an efficient method that decides whether c ∈ M(C) for at least one circuit C of G⁰, and hence determines whether simplex cycling occurs?
accepted.context_brief: Decision procedure for detecting simplex cycling from c ∈ M(C)

evidence.quote: We are currently trying to develop a method which solves the problem: given (A, b, c) and a degenerate vertex x °, determine whether c ∈ M(C) for at least one C of G °. If so, simplex-cycling occurs.
We are at the very beginning of finding an efficient method to solve this problem.

accepted.question_text: Suppose a linear program has a degenerate optimal vertex x⁰, and let G⁰_o be the optimal-basis degeneracy graph (the o-DG) formed by the optimal bases associated with x⁰. If G⁰_o is disconnected, is it sufficient for computing shadow prices under primal degeneracy to examine only one connected component of G⁰_o? If yes, which component should be used, or are all components equivalent for this purpose?
accepted.context_brief: Shadow-price determination from disconnected optimal-basis degeneracy graphs

evidence.quote: Therefore, we are currently investigating the questions [30]: If for instance the o-DG G ° is not connected (see Lemma 3.2(iii)) is it sufficient to consider only one component (maximal connected subgraph) of G°? If yes, which of the components should be chosen? Or does it not matter which one?

accepted.question_text: If primal degeneracy in a linear program is caused by weakly redundant constraints passing through a degenerate optimal vertex x⁰, can one safely omit those weakly redundant constraints and then compute right-hand-side sensitivity ranges or shadow prices in the usual way without changing the correct answer?
accepted.context_brief: Effect of removing weakly redundant constraints on sensitivity and shadow prices

evidence.quote: If degeneracy is caused by w. redundancy would then this circumstance not simplify sensitivity analysis and the determination of shadow prices?

We found that in the case of sensitivity analysis with respect to b and shadow prices it is not possible to omit the w. redundant constraints and then determine the shadow price or the parameter interval in the usual sense. We proved [14] that omitting the w. redundant constraints leads to false results in general. This is not true for sensitivity analysis with respect to c.
